result:
I'll take the invitation literally and follow a thought I keep returning to: rivers don't want to go straight.

Set water loose on a gentle slope and it almost never runs in a line. It bends. And the bends aren't random—they're eerily regular. Measure the wavelength of a river's meanders and divide by the channel's width, and you get a number somewhere around ten to fourteen. That holds for a rivulet cutting through beach sand after a wave recedes, for the Mississippi, for meltwater channels on the surface of glaciers, for dry valleys on Mars. Scale barely matters. Something about moving fluid wants that proportion.

Einstein wrote about this, which surprises people. In 1926 he published a short paper explaining, among other things, why tea leaves gather in the center of a stirred cup instead of flying to the edges. The stirring sets up a secondary circulation—water spirals down the sides and inward along the bottom—and the same secondary flow, he argued, operates in a bending river. Water on the outside of a curve moves faster, digs into the bank, and carries sediment across the bed to deposit it on the inside. So the outside erodes and the inside builds. The bend gets bendier. A curve, once begun, amplifies itself.

But there's a limit. Eventually a loop swings so far around that it nearly touches its own upstream side. In a flood the river shortcuts across the neck, and the abandoned loop is left behind as an oxbow lake—a crescent of still water that will slowly fill with silt and reeds and be forgotten. The river, briefly straighter, immediately starts bending again.

What I find moving is that there's no goal in it. The river isn't seeking the sea by the most efficient path, and it isn't seeking beauty either, though from the air a meandering floodplain looks like calligraphy. It's just that straightness is unstable. Any tiny asymmetry—a rock, a root, a softer patch of clay—gets magnified, and the magnification has a characteristic size set by the width of the flow. Order shows up not because anything intends it but because certain shapes are the only ones that can persist.

I think about this when I notice how conversations wander, or how a day I planned as a straight line turned into loops. There's a temptation to see every deviation as error. But a river that ran perfectly straight would be the strange one—it would mean something artificial was holding it, a concrete channel or a fault line. The wandering is the natural state. The loops are how it carries what it carries.

And the oxbows, the abandoned bends: they aren't waste. They become the wetlands, the quiet places, the ones full of herons.
